title: 40 Outdoor Activities Every Kid Should Do Before They’re 12
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Martinko begins with the disappearance of nature words from our language, citing Miles Richardson's 2025 study that found a 60% decline in nature-related words in books between 1800 and 2019, and a National Trust study showing words like tweet, web and stream captured by technology. Her argument is that the linguistic loss matters because if we do not talk about nature we stop thinking about it and stop going out in it, and children inherit their parents' disconnection. She then makes the developmental case for outdoor time, where children test their bodies, take risks, build strength and regulate intense emotions, quoting Erika Christakis on doubling outdoor play. Because nature has to become a desirable destination, she endorses the National Trust's 50 things to do before you're 11 and three quarters campaign, based on the idea that interests formed before twelve tend to last. The heart of the piece is her own list of forty activities, from building snow forts and stacking firewood to watching the ice go out of a lake. She closes by arguing that repetition turns outdoor time into a habit that eventually needs no supervision.
points: Richardson attributes the decline in nature words to urbanization, environmental degradation and a failure of intergenerational transmission.
Only 1% of uses of the word tweet in the National Trust study referred to birdsong, showing how technology has colonized nature vocabulary.
Martinko calls outdoor play a near-magical tool for resolving restlessness, boredom and intense emotions in children.
The age twelve cutoff reflects research suggesting skills and hobbies formed before then are more likely to persist into adulthood.
Her list mixes adventures like caves and meteor showers with chores like digging potatoes and stacking wood.
quotes: A study published in a journal called Earth in July 2025 found a 60% decline in the use of nature-related words between 1800 and 2019.
As parents lose connection to nature, their children begin life with lower connection, creating cultural inertia that persists even if environmental conditions improve.
This might just seem like a minor socio-linguistic amusement, but there’s a larger issue here. If we don’t talk about nature, we stop thinking about nature.
They learn to test the limits of their bodies, take physical risks, be brave and bold, and use their imaginations to come up with games.

But in order to do that, nature needs to be positioned as a desirable destination. It must be a place in which a child has spent sufficient time to be able to recognize how good it makes them feel—and to want more of it.
Because research suggests that if kids get hooked on an activity or develop a new skill or hobby before the age of 12, they’re more likely to stick with it or return to it later.
Before you know it, a day won’t feel right without a good chunk of it devoted to outdoor play, and soon they’ll be out there on their own, no longer needing supervision or guidance.
